title: "blessed are the poor in spirit"
hookLine: "blessed are the poor in spirit" — the upside-down list
tomorrow: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling

cards: Hashtag blessed. It turns up under the new car, the beach photo, the engagement ring. Now a hillside in Galilee.
Crowds have followed a teacher out of the towns, many of them sick. He sits down and starts a long talk with a list of who's blessed. And every name on it is the one you wouldn't expect.
The poor. The ones who are crying. The gentle ones who never win an argument.
It opens what Christians call the Sermon on the Mount.

teach.b: They're called the Beatitudes, from the Latin word for blessed. In Matthew's Gospel they're usually counted as eight, and each has the same shape: blessed are these people, because this will happen to them.

The first, in the old English: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The second: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Then the meek, who will inherit the earth.
The hungry for what's right. The merciful. The pure in heart.
The peacemakers. And the people hounded for doing right. Then the word itself.
The Greek word for blessed, makarioi, wasn't a churchy word. In ordinary Greek it described the fortunate, the happy. Old poets even used it for the gods, who had nothing to worry about.
So the sentence lands like this: the lucky ones are the broke ones. The lucky ones are the ones at the funeral. It's meant to make you blink.
Another Gospel has a shorter, blunter version: blessed are you poor, with no in spirit at all. Poor in money, poor in pride, or both: Christians have long talked about the difference.
Either way, the list turns the ladder over.
Later Jesus says it in a way that became a saying: "the last shall be first, and the first last."

how: Christians read the Beatitudes as a guide for daily life. In the Catholic calendar they're the Gospel reading on All Saints' Day, and in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they're often sung.

s: the Beatitudes are ten rules, like the commandments
Matthew's list is usually counted as eight, and none is a rule. each one says who's fortunate, and why.
another Gospel has a shorter, blunter version
Luke simply says: blessed are you poor. no "in spirit."
the Greek word for blessed was also used for the gods
makarioi meant fortunate, carefree. old poets used it for the gods. Matthew pins it on the poor and the grieving.

games.q: a teacher sits down on a hillside in front of a crowd of ordinary, struggling people. who does his first sentence call blessed?
o: the rich, because they've been rewarded.
the ones who keep every rule.
games.why: "blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." the list starts at the bottom, and it stays there.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let one long breath out. Think of one person you tend to overlook.
Not someone you dislike; someone you just don't see. The person who cleans the building. The quiet one in the group chat.
Hold their face in your mind. If you pray, you can hold them there the way you would in a prayer. If you don't, just let them be first in your mind for a little while.

wordCard.voice: The Beatitudes. Eight blessings that start at the bottom. Fourteenth word. Amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes: that's week two.

orig.note: Greek. blessed, fortunate, happy. every Beatitude in Matthew opens with it.

carryVoice: Your line: the last shall be first. Week three brings love, faith, songs that shout, a cross and an empty tomb. Day fourteen.
